newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's stability assured, PM tells investors.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's stability assured, PM tells investors.

text.p: Prime Minister Gyula Horn said on Tuesday that Hungary has reoriented itself towards the West and told investors that stability was assured whoever wins next year's elections.

Horn, speaking at what was billed as a summit conference for investors, told an audience of more than 100 businessmen, diplomats and officials that Hungary no longer needed drastic economic restructuring.

A shock austerity programme already in place had stabilised the economy and had prompted a resumption of economic growth, he said. Inflation should fall from more than 30 percent to an anticipated 13 to 13.5 percent year on year next year.

"We are close to the average of the lower-income member states of the European Union," said Horn, whose Socialist Party and allied Free Democrats who will be defending a 72 percent majority in parliament at next May's elections.
"No matter what the outcome of the elections, there should be continuity that has characterised Hungarian economic growth so far," Horn told his audience.
He said Hungary had worked to normalise ties with its neighbours, played a stabilising role in the region and created stable political conditions within Hungary.

"Our government that has been in power for the last 34 months has freed itself and the population of ideological governance," said Horn, whose Socialists are the successors to the communists who once ruled Hungary.
He said Hungary's push for Euro-Atlantic integration by seeking EU and NATO membership should reassure investors.
"It is important for investors because it makes their presence here more secure and safe," Horn said.
"And with our neighbours we do not talk about historical grievances," he added. "We have to deal with how to cooperate with our neighbours."

Judit Csiha, Hungary's privatisation minister and head of the APV Rt privatisation agency, said Hungary had succeeded in privatisation by quickly selling strategic sectors such as banks and telecommunications.
"More or less we can state that the privatisation process has fulfilled its responsibility. We have come to the end of this process," Csiha said.
"Throughout the past years we have (generated) $16 billion capital revenues, partly as cash revenues, partly as development investment.

"Investors fulfil all their undertakings and obligations. At the same time it is important to mention that with the employees' share programme and...the compensation vouchers exchange...domestic private ownership has significantly increased," she said.

Csiha said the main focus of APV for the immediate future would be bolstering medium and small enterprises and shepherding a plan through parliament to allow for long-term management of companies that are to remain in state hands

Charles McVeigh, chairman of Salomon Brothers International, said Horn's comments "would be welcomed by the international financial community" but noted that Hungary needed to expand its base of small and medium-sized businesses.
He said these would "spread growth across different regions and different levels of income", making more Hungarians feel part of the country's economic boom.
